primary_artifact: /Volumes/HMI-Library/heavy-metal-index-raw/reports/EFSA Journal - 2020 -  - Update of the risk assessment of nickel in food and drinking water.pdf
disposition_reason: The 2020 EFSA nickel update discusses cocoa/chocolate only qualitatively in the main PDF (chocolate drives 'Sugar and confectionary' occurrence and exposure contributions); the cocoa-specific occurrence statistics are in Annex C (separate file), and the only cocoa numbers printed are recalled 2015 values and cited literature.

study.design: monitoring summary and dietary exposure assessment (EFSA scientific opinion)
study.material_scope: chocolate (cocoa) products, cocoa beans/cocoa products (only qualitatively in PDF)
study.growing_origin_vs_market: EU monitoring (26 countries); origin not reported
study.sampling_unit: individual analytical results (48,007 total after cleaning, all foods and water)
study.lod_loq: Annex C Table C.3 (not in PDF)
study.basis: as sold; solids diluted for exposure

exposure.statement: TDI for nickel (chronic), based on BMDL10 1.3 mg/kg bw/day for post-implantation loss in rats.
Acute reference point: LOAEL for eczematous flare-up in nickel-sensitised humans; MOE approach (MOE >=30 indicates low concern).

High mean nickel levels in 'Sugar and confectionary' are mainly driven by chocolate (cocoa) products, and in 'Vegetables and vegetable products' by cocoa beans/cocoa products, tea leaves and seaweed (statistics only in Annex C).

'Sugar and confectionary' contributed up to 31% of mean LB chronic Ni exposure in adolescents, mostly driven by chocolate (cocoa) products; cocoa beverages and soft drinks were the main non-alcoholic beverage contributors for toddlers, other children and adolescents.

Chocolate was among the most relevant food categories for P95 UB acute nickel exposure in most surveys (with beans, coffee, ready-to-eat soups, breakfast cereals); for other children and adolescents beans and chocolate were the most relevant.
French infant/toddler TDS (Sirot et al., 2018, cited): chocolate-based products contributed 30-60% of Ni dietary exposure for 13-36-month-old children.

French infant TDS (Chekri et al., 2019, cited): high mean Ni in biscuits/bars (527 µg/kg, n=1), dairy desserts (388), pastries (173) and hot beverages (96.2) mainly due to samples containing chocolate.
2015 CONTAM values recalled: chocolate (cocoa) products ~3,800 µg/kg; cocoa beans and cocoa products ~9,500 µg/kg.
Solid forms of cocoa powder, cocoa powder preparations and cocoa beans were adjusted by dilution factors and reclassified to liquid forms for exposure.

contradictions_with_stored_summary: None found on cocoa; stored summary does not state that cocoa-specific statistics are only in Annex C.
